comments.author: cthor
comments.story: Fran Blanche: This Is Not Legal
comments.why: Prior example of self-claiming through online music labels
comments.text: The self-claiming thing has at least been done already (through the use of online music labels): < [LINK] > and < [VIDEO] > YouTube doesn't let just anyone make ContentID claims and start trolling. You do need to jump through a few hoops to get an air of legitimacy first.

comments.author: norswap
comments.story: Explaining copyright broke the YouTube copyright system
comments.why: Shows creators circumventing the system by claiming their own videos
comments.text: The situation is now so silly that some people are circumventing the system by copyright claiming their own videos: [VIDEO] This enable them to at least get some of the revenue of their video (by sharing with other (often bogus) claimants), and to monetize re-uploads (something normally available only to big channels). Why Google doesn't do anything about this mess is beyond me.

comments.author: Veedrac
comments.story: Explaining copyright broke the YouTube copyright system
comments.why: Example of how easily the claim system can be gamed
comments.text: It's not just that it's easy, but that the theft is legal and profitable. You don't even need to be rich to do this, you just need stuff you can claim; see How to Break YouTube (Copyright Claim your own video). [VIDEO]

comments.author: kristofferR
comments.story: Warner music claimed my video for defending their copyright [video]
comments.why: Self-claiming your own video via ContentID to block abusers
comments.text: There is actually something creators can do about it. If you add your own copyrighted song to ContentID and add the song to your video, you can copyright claim your own video and prevent others from abusing ContentID to earn money on it. [VIDEO]
